# Overview

## What the Environment Factory is

Every E2E test needs data. A test for "user adds item to cart" needs a user, products, and a cart. A test for "admin views analytics" needs an organization with users, runs, and history.

Tests can't share data -- if one test deletes a product, another test that expects 10 products will fail. When tests run in parallel, this gets worse.

The Environment Factory solves this. It's a single POST endpoint in your backend that the Autonoma platform calls to:

1. Create fresh, isolated data before each test run
2. Tear down that data after the test finishes

Each test run gets its own organization, users, and data. No interference between tests.

## What the SDK does

The Autonoma SDK is a set of packages that you install in your backend. Together they implement the entire Environment Factory endpoint. You configure it with your database connection, a scope field, two secrets, and an auth callback.

The SDK handles everything:
- Reading your database schema (models, fields, relationships)
- Creating records in the correct FK order automatically
- Tearing down all created data without leaving orphans
- Verifying incoming request signatures (HMAC-SHA256)
- Signing teardown tokens so nobody can tamper with them
- Blocking the endpoint in production by default

You write minimal configuration code. The SDK does the rest.

SDKs are available for TypeScript, Python, and Elixir. Each language provides a core protocol library, ORM adapters (for your database layer), and server/framework adapters (for your HTTP framework). You install one of each.

## The three actions

The endpoint handles three actions via POST:

discover -- The platform asks "what does your database look like?" The SDK reads your ORM schema and returns the models, fields, and relationships. The platform uses this to generate valid scenario data.

up -- The platform sends scenario data (a nested tree describing what records to create). The SDK creates them in the correct FK order and returns auth credentials so the test runner can log in. It also returns a signed token for teardown.

down -- The platform sends the signed token back. The SDK verifies it and deletes everything that was created -- in the correct order, without FK constraint violations.

## What you provide

adapter       Your ORM adapter configured with a scope field.
sharedSecret  A secret shared between you and Autonoma -- verifies incoming requests.
signingSecret A secret only you know -- signs the teardown token so nobody can tamper with it.
auth          A callback that creates real login credentials for test users.

## The scope field

Most multi-tenant apps have a foreign key like organizationId on every model. This is the "scope field" -- it's how the SDK isolates test data.

During creation: child records get the organization's ID automatically via nesting. You never set it manually -- the SDK reads the FK graph and injects it.

During teardown: the SDK deletes everything where the scope field equals the test organization's ID, in reverse FK order to avoid constraint violations.

Example: if your database has Organization, User, and Application models, and both User and Application have an organizationId column pointing to Organization, then organizationId is your scope field. The SDK will:
1. Create the Organization first
2. Create Users and Applications with organizationId set to the Organization's ID
3. On teardown, delete Applications, then Users, then the Organization

If your app isn't multi-tenant, you'll need a dedicated field (like testRunId) on every model.

Limitation: The scope field must be a single column. Compound scope keys (e.g., organizationId + countryId) are not supported. If your app scopes by multiple fields, use a single root entity with its own ID that child models reference.

## The two secrets

You need two different secrets. The SDK will throw an error if they are the same.

Shared secret (AUTONOMA_SHARED_SECRET): Both you and Autonoma know this. Autonoma signs every request with HMAC-SHA256; your endpoint verifies the signature. This prevents unauthorized calls to your endpoint.

Signing secret (AUTONOMA_SIGNING_SECRET): Only you know this. During up, the SDK signs a token containing the IDs of all created records. During down, it verifies the token before deleting. Even Autonoma can't forge or modify this token -- they just store it and pass it back.

Generate both with different values:

  openssl rand -hex 32   # use as AUTONOMA_SHARED_SECRET
  openssl rand -hex 32   # use as AUTONOMA_SIGNING_SECRET (must be different!)

## Handling updates

The platform sends scenario data inline in the up request. If your schema changes (you add a model, rename a field), the platform sees the change on the next discover call. There are no local files to keep in sync.

## SDK availability

SDKs are available for three languages:

TypeScript -- ORM adapters for Prisma and Drizzle. Server adapters for Web standard (Next.js, Hono, Bun, Deno), Express, and Node.js http.

Python -- ORM adapters for SQLAlchemy and other Python ORMs. Server adapters for popular Python web frameworks.

Elixir -- ORM adapters for Ecto. Server adapters for Phoenix and Plug.

Each language follows the same architecture: a core protocol library plus ORM and server adapter packages. The protocol behavior is identical across languages -- only the package names and syntax differ.

See the language-specific documentation in each SDK directory for installation instructions and code examples.


---

# Autonoma Environment Factory Protocol

## Overview

The Environment Factory protocol defines how the Autonoma platform communicates with your backend to create and destroy isolated test data. It is a simple request-response protocol over HTTP POST with HMAC-SHA256 authentication.

Protocol version: 1.0

## Transport

All communication happens over a single HTTP POST endpoint. The URL is chosen by you (e.g., /api/autonoma). The platform sends JSON requests and expects JSON responses.

## Authentication

Every request is authenticated with HMAC-SHA256. The platform computes the signature over the raw request body using the shared secret and includes it in the x-signature header.

The SDK verifies the signature before processing any request. If the signature is missing or invalid, the request is rejected with a 401 status.

### The two secrets

The protocol uses two separate secrets. They must be different values.

Shared secret: Known by both the Autonoma platform and your backend. Used for HMAC-SHA256 request signing. The platform signs; your SDK verifies.

Signing secret: Known only by your backend. Used to sign the refs token during up and verify it during down. The platform stores this token opaquely and passes it back -- it cannot read or modify it.

## Request format

Every request is an HTTP POST with:
- Content-Type: application/json
- x-signature: HMAC-SHA256 hex digest of the raw body, keyed with the shared secret

The request body is a JSON object with an "action" field that determines the operation.

## Response format

Every response is a JSON object. Successful responses include metadata fields:

  version   The protocol version string (currently "1.0").
  sdk       An object with language, orm, and server fields identifying the SDK implementation.

Error responses include:

  error     A human-readable error message.
  code      A machine-readable error code string.

## Actions

### discover

Request:

  {
    "action": "discover"
  }

Response (200):

  {
    "version": "1.0",
    "sdk": { "language": "typescript", "orm": "prisma", "server": "web" },
    "schema": {
      "models": [ ... ],
      "edges": [ ... ],
      "relations": [ ... ],
      "scopeField": "organizationId"
    }
  }

The schema object contains:
- models: list of all database models with their fields (name, type, required, id, hasDefault)
- edges: list of all FK relationships (from model, to model, local field, foreign field, nullable)
- relations: named relation mappings used for scenario nesting
- scopeField: the field name used for test data isolation

### up

Request:

  {
    "action": "up",
    "testRunId": "optional-uuid",
    "create": {
      "ModelName": [{ "field": "value", ... }]
    }
  }

If testRunId is omitted, the SDK generates a random UUID.

The create field contains a nested JSON tree describing what records to create. See scenarios.txt for the full format.

Response (200):

  {
    "version": "1.0",
    "sdk": { "language": "typescript", "orm": "prisma", "server": "web" },
    "auth": { "token": "...", "cookies": [...], "credentials": {...} },
    "refs": {
      "ModelName": [{ "id": "...", "field": "value", ... }]
    },
    "refsToken": "header.payload.signature"
  }

- auth: credentials for the test runner to authenticate (format depends on auth callback)
- refs: all created records, keyed by model name
- refsToken: a signed token encoding the created record IDs, used for teardown

### down

Request:

  {
    "action": "down",
    "refsToken": "header.payload.signature"
  }

The refsToken is the exact token returned by the up response.

Response (200):

  {
    "version": "1.0",
    "sdk": { "language": "typescript", "orm": "prisma", "server": "web" },
    "ok": true
  }

## The scope field

The scope field is a single column name (e.g., organizationId) present on most models in the database. It references a root entity (e.g., Organization) that acts as the isolation boundary for test data.

During up: the SDK creates the root entity first, then injects the scope field value into all child records.

During teardown: the SDK deletes all records matching the scope field value, in reverse topological order to respect FK constraints. Records on models without the scope field are deleted by their individual IDs from the refs token.

## The refs token

The refs token is a JWT-like structure (header.payload.signature) signed with the signing secret. It contains:
- The test run ID (scope value)
- All created record IDs, keyed by model name

The token is signed by the SDK during up and verified during down. Because only your backend knows the signing secret, the token cannot be forged or modified by the platform or any external party. This ensures that down can only delete records that up created.

## Safety model

The protocol enforces hard safety constraints:

1. BLOCKED IN PRODUCTION
   The endpoint returns 404 when the application is running in production mode (unless explicitly opted in with an allowProduction flag). This prevents accidental use against production databases.

2. UP CAN ONLY CREATE
   The up action uses the ORM's create operations. It cannot update, delete, drop, truncate, or execute raw SQL. The worst it can do is insert rows.

3. DOWN CAN ONLY DELETE WHAT UP CREATED
   During up, the SDK signs a token with the IDs of every created record using your signing secret. During down, the SDK verifies that token before deleting. It deletes only the records listed in the token. Even the Autonoma platform cannot forge or modify this token.

4. REQUESTS ARE AUTHENTICATED
   Every request is HMAC-SHA256 signed with the shared secret. Unsigned or tampered requests are rejected with 401.

5. NO RAW SQL
   All database operations go through the ORM layer. The SDK calls ORM create and delete methods, never raw SQL strings. Schema validation happens at the ORM level.

## Error codes

  Code                  HTTP Status  Meaning
  INVALID_SIGNATURE     401          HMAC signature missing or does not match
  INVALID_BODY          400          Request body is not valid JSON, or missing required fields
  UNKNOWN_ACTION        400          The action field is not discover, up, or down
  UNKNOWN_ENVIRONMENT   400          The requested environment name does not exist
  INVALID_REFS_TOKEN    403          The refs token is missing, malformed, or signature verification failed
  PRODUCTION_BLOCKED    404          Endpoint is disabled in production mode
  SAME_SECRETS          500          sharedSecret and signingSecret are the same value
  INTERNAL_ERROR        500          Unexpected server error

## HMAC signature computation

The signature is computed as:

  HMAC-SHA256(raw_request_body_bytes, shared_secret) -> hex digest

The platform sends this as the x-signature header value. The SDK recomputes the HMAC over the raw body string (before JSON parsing) and compares using a constant-time comparison.

Important: the signature is computed over the exact bytes of the request body. The server adapter must extract the raw body as a string before any JSON parsing or middleware transformation.


---

# Writing Scenario Data

Scenario data describes what database records to create. The Autonoma platform generates this from your schema, but you may write it for integration tests and debugging.

## Why not raw SQL?

The Environment Factory is designed with hard constraints that make it safe by construction:

1. BLOCKED IN PRODUCTION
   Endpoint returns 404 when the application is in production mode (unless explicitly opted in).

2. UP CAN ONLY CREATE
   The up action calls ORM create methods. It cannot UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, TRUNCATE, or run raw SQL. The worst it can do is INSERT rows.

3. DOWN CAN ONLY DELETE WHAT UP CREATED
   During up, the SDK signs a token with the IDs of every created record, using your signing secret (not the shared secret). During down, the SDK verifies that token before deleting. It deletes only the records listed in the token. Even Autonoma cannot forge or modify this token.

4. REQUESTS ARE AUTHENTICATED
   Every request is HMAC-SHA256 signed with the shared secret. Unsigned or tampered requests are rejected with 401.

5. NO RAW SQL
   All database operations go through your ORM. The SDK uses ORM create and delete methods, not SQL strings. Schema validation happens at the ORM level.

Contrast with raw SQL: a raw SQL endpoint could DROP TABLE, DELETE FROM users, or UPDATE users SET role = 'admin'. Even with auth, one malformed query could destroy production data. The Environment Factory can't do any of that.

This is why scenario data is a structured JSON tree, not SQL. The SDK interprets it as a series of ORM create calls -- nothing more.

## The format

Data is a nested JSON tree. The top-level keys are model names from your database schema. Children are nested inside their parents. The SDK reads FK relationships from your ORM schema and wires IDs automatically -- you never set FK fields manually.

Think of it like Protocol Buffers: the schema is shared once (via discover), and after that the data contains only values -- no field types, no FK directions, no column names. Both sides already know the structure. The platform calls discover to learn your schema, then sends scenario data that references models and relation names. Your SDK already has the same schema from your ORM, so it knows exactly how to interpret the nesting and wire the foreign keys.

All field values must be complete and literal -- the SDK does not perform any template resolution or variable substitution. The platform is responsible for generating fully resolved data before sending it.

### Minimal example (org + user)

  {
    "create": {
      "Organization": [{
        "name": "Test Org",
        "slug": "test-org",
        "members": [{
          "role": "owner",
          "user": [{ "name": "Admin", "email": "admin@test.com" }]
        }]
      }]
    }
  }

This creates:
1. One Organization
2. One User (created first because Member holds the FK to it)
3. One Member with organizationId set to the Organization's ID and userId set to the User's ID

### How does the SDK know which FK to set?

It doesn't guess. The ORM adapter reads your schema metadata at runtime and extracts every model, field, and relationship -- including the exact FK column names.

For example, given a schema where:
- Organization has a one-to-many relation to Member
- Member has a column organizationId pointing to Organization.id
- Member has a column userId pointing to User.id

The adapter extracts:
- Organization.members is a relation to Member
- Member holds the FK column organizationId pointing to Organization.id
- Member.user is a relation to User
- Member holds the FK column userId pointing to User.id

Each ORM adapter reads this metadata differently -- Prisma embeds it in the generated client, Drizzle exports it as plain objects, SQLAlchemy exposes it via inspection, Ecto reads it from schema modules -- but they all produce the same result. The SDK receives a standardized schema map and uses it to wire every nested object automatically.

The FK column name comes directly from your schema definition -- whether you called it organizationId, orgId, tenant_fk, or anything else. No string matching, no conventions, no guessing.

### Realistic example (org with apps, tests, runs)

  {
    "create": {
      "Organization": [{
        "name": "Acme Corp",
        "slug": "acme-corp",

        "members": [
          { "role": "owner", "user": [{ "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@test.com" }] },
          { "role": "admin", "user": [{ "name": "Bob", "email": "bob@test.com" }] }
        ],

        "applications": [
          {
            "_alias": "webApp",
            "name": "Marketing Website",
            "architecture": "WEB",
            "webApplicationData": [{ "url": "https://acme.com" }],
            "tags": [
              { "name": "Critical", "color": "#DC2626" },
              { "name": "Flaky", "color": "#EAB308" }
            ]
          },
          {
            "name": "Android App",
            "architecture": "ANDROID",
            "mobileApplicationData": [{ "packageUrl": "https://cdn.example.com/app.apk" }]
          }
        ]
      }]
    }
  }

## How nesting works

The SDK reads your ORM schema's relations to know what each nested key means. The nested key must be the exact relation field name from the parent model in your ORM schema.

### Finding the right relation name

Look at the parent model in your ORM schema. The relation field names on the parent are the keys you use in scenario nesting. For example, if Organization has relation fields named members, applications, and invitations, use those exact names in your scenario JSON.

Warning: some schemas use PascalCase for relation names (e.g., Application instead of applications). Always check your ORM schema.

### FK direction: child FK vs parent FK

The SDK handles both FK directions:

FK on child (most common): Application.organizationId points to Organization.
- Parent (Organization) is created first
- Child (Application) is created after, with organizationId set automatically
- In the scenario, nest Application under Organization

FK on parent (reverse): Member.userId points to User.
- The FK (userId) is on Member, but User is the child in the nesting
- The SDK detects this: creates User first, then sets Member.userId
- In the scenario, nest User under Member

This is how you solve the "member-user distribution" problem -- each member gets its own user, correctly wired.

## What to include in fields

Required: every field marked as required in your schema that does NOT have a default value, is not auto-generated, and is not an auto-updated timestamp.

Unique fields: must have unique values to avoid collisions when tests run in parallel.

  { "name": "Acme Corp", "slug": "acme-corp", "email": "admin@test.com" }

## What to omit

- id -- auto-generated by the database
- Fields with default values -- the database or ORM handles them
- Auto-updated timestamp fields -- handled by the ORM automatically
- FK fields handled by nesting -- if you nest Application under Organization, don't set organizationId manually
- The scope field -- the SDK injects it automatically for models that have it

Example: given a model with fields id (auto-generated), name (required), architecture (required enum), organizationId (FK), createdAt (default now), and updatedAt (auto-updated), you only provide name and architecture:

  { "name": "My App", "architecture": "WEB" }

The SDK handles id, organizationId, createdAt, and updatedAt.

## Cross-branch references (_alias / _ref)

When a record needs a FK to something in a different branch of the tree, use _alias to name a node and _ref to reference it.

### Problem: TestGeneration needs applicationId

TestGeneration is nested under TestPlan, but it also needs applicationId which points to the Application (a different branch):

  Organization
  +-- Application (webApp)       <- need to reference this
  |   +-- TestPlan
  |       +-- TestGeneration     <- needs applicationId = webApp.id

### Solution: _alias + _ref

  {
    "applications": [{
      "_alias": "webApp",
      "name": "Marketing Website",
      "architecture": "WEB",

      "testPlans": [{
        "name": "Smoke Plan",
        "plan": "content",
        "testGenerations": [{
          "_alias": "gen1",
          "conversation": "[]",
          "status": "success",
          "applicationId": { "_ref": "webApp" }
        }]
      }],

      "tests": [{
        "name": "Homepage Test",
        "testGenerationId": { "_ref": "gen1" },
        "steps": [
          { "order": 1, "interaction": "click", "params": {} }
        ]
      }]
    }]
  }

Rules:
- _alias is a string name you choose. It must be unique across the entire scenario.
- _ref resolves to the id of the aliased node after it's created.
- The aliased node must appear before the _ref in tree traversal order (depth-first). If it doesn't, you'll get: _ref "xyz" not found.
- You can chain references: alias a node, then reference it from multiple places.

### Another example: Invitation with inviterId

  {
    "Organization": [{
      "name": "Org",
      "members": [{
        "role": "owner",
        "user": [{
          "_alias": "inviter",
          "name": "Alice",
          "email": "alice@test.com"
        }]
      }],
      "invitations": [
        { "email": "bob@test.com", "inviterId": { "_ref": "inviter" }, "role": "admin", "expiresAt": "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z" },
        { "email": "carol@test.com", "inviterId": { "_ref": "inviter" }, "role": "member", "expiresAt": "2025-01-01T00:00:00Z" }
      ]
    }]
  }

### Another example: TestTag (join table)

  {
    "applications": [{
      "tags": [
        { "_alias": "tag1", "name": "Critical", "color": "#FF0000" },
        { "_alias": "tag2", "name": "High", "color": "#FF8800" }
      ],
      "tests": [{
        "name": "Test",
        "testTags": [
          { "tagId": { "_ref": "tag1" } },
          { "tagId": { "_ref": "tag2" } }
        ]
      }]
    }]
  }

## The three standard scenarios

When writing scenarios for a project, create three:

### empty -- Org + user only
Tests empty states, onboarding flows, "no data yet" screens.

  {
    "create": {
      "Organization": [{
        "name": "Empty Org",
        "slug": "empty-org",
        "members": [{ "role": "owner", "user": [{ "name": "Solo User", "email": "solo@test.com" }] }]
      }]
    }
  }

### standard -- Realistic variety
Enough data to test every filter, status, and category. Use descriptive names ("Marketing Website", not "App 1"). Include at least one entity per enum value.

  {
    "create": {
      "Organization": [{
        "name": "Acme Corp",
        "slug": "acme-corp",
        "members": [
          { "role": "owner", "user": [{ "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@test.com" }] },
          { "role": "admin", "user": [{ "name": "Bob", "email": "bob@test.com" }] },
          { "role": "viewer", "user": [{ "name": "Carol", "email": "carol@test.com" }] }
        ],
        "applications": [
          {
            "_alias": "webApp",
            "name": "Marketing Website",
            "architecture": "WEB",
            "tags": [
              { "name": "Critical", "color": "#DC2626" },
              { "name": "P1 - High", "color": "#F97316" },
              { "name": "Flaky", "color": "#EAB308" }
            ]
          },
          { "name": "Android App", "architecture": "ANDROID" },
          { "name": "iOS App", "architecture": "IOS" }
        ]
      }]
    }
  }

### large -- High volume
Exceeds pagination thresholds. Tests pagination, sort stability, filter performance. Each record is explicitly listed in the array.

  {
    "create": {
      "Organization": [{
        "name": "Load Test Org",
        "slug": "load-test",
        "members": [{ "role": "owner", "user": [{ "name": "User", "email": "load@test.com" }] }],
        "applications": [{
          "_alias": "app",
          "name": "App",
          "architecture": "WEB",
          "tags": [
            { "name": "Tag 1", "color": "#333" },
            { "name": "Tag 2", "color": "#333" },
            { "name": "Tag 3", "color": "#333" }
          ],
          "testPlans": [{
            "name": "Plan",
            "plan": "x",
            "testGenerations": [{
              "_alias": "gen1",
              "conversation": "[]",
              "applicationId": { "_ref": "app" }
            }]
          }],
          "tests": [{
            "name": "Test",
            "testGenerationId": { "_ref": "gen1" }
          }]
        }]
      }]
    }
  }
